title: Diamond Price and Cut
text:
What the data show
The chart shows a clear pattern: larger diamonds cost more, and the strength of that relationship depends on the cut. In this dataset, price rises sharply as carat increases, while the spread by cut suggests that quality and craftsmanship matter alongside stone size.
This example is based on real observations from a public data set, not on invented values or illustrative modeling assumptions. The graphic is therefore a valid data-based analysis, not a planning illustration.
A simple summary of the same data helps show the pattern even more directly:


# A tibble: 5 × 4
  cut       mean_price mean_carat     n
  <ord>          <dbl>      <dbl> <int>
1 Fair           4359.      1.05   1610
2 Good           3929.      0.849  4906
3 Very Good      3982.      0.806 12082
4 Premium        4584.      0.892 13791
5 Ideal          3458.      0.703 21551


The table confirms that the average price is not constant across cuts, and the relationship between cut and value is visible in real measurements from the data set.
